report.summary: Global law firm Latham & Watkins has purchased Nvidia servers to run AI models in-house, signalling a shift toward private, on-premises AI infrastructure in professional services.
report.background: Law firms handle privileged, highly confidential client material, which makes public cloud AI tools a hard sell for general counsels and compliance teams. Through 2023-2024, most firms adopted legal-specific AI copilots such as Harvey, CoCounsel and Legora built on top of third-party models hosted by OpenAI, Anthropic or Microsoft Azure. That arrangement leaves firms dependent on vendor terms, data-retention policies and per-seat pricing. Meanwhile Nvidia's enterprise DGX and HGX server lines, built around H100/H200 GPUs, have become the standard hardware for private model hosting, and supply constraints have eased enough for non-tech buyers to procure them. Latham & Watkins, one of the world's highest-grossing firms with thousands of lawyers, buying its own compute is an early signal that large professional-services organisations now see AI infrastructure as a strategic asset rather than a subscription line item.
key_points: Latham & Watkins is purchasing Nvidia server hardware to run AI models on its own infrastructure, rather than routing sensitive legal work through third-party cloud APIs.

The driver is confidentiality: client privilege and data-residency rules make on-premises or private-cloud inference far easier to justify to clients and regulators than sending documents to external model providers.
It marks a shift in legal AI procurement, from renting capabilities via vendors like Harvey or CoCounsel to owning the underlying compute and fine-tuned models.
Nvidia's enterprise server business benefits, since demand for private GPU capacity now comes from law, finance and healthcare, not just hyperscalers and AI startups.

Running models internally is capital-intensive and operationally demanding: firms need GPU capacity planning, security hardening, model-update pipelines and ML engineering talent they have never had to hire before.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is another data point that inference is decentralising: high-value, confidentiality-sensitive enterprises increasingly want weights, not APIs. That benefits Nvidia's enterprise server line, private-cloud providers and open-weight model ecosystems, while creating a new competitor to SaaS legal-AI vendors who charge per seat on top of rented compute. For developers, it means more jobs building RAG pipelines, evaluation harnesses and fine-tuning workflows inside conservative, compliance-heavy organisations, plus growing demand for skills in vLLM-style serving and GPU operations. For regular users, expect law firms to move faster on document review, drafting and diligence, but with tighter guardrails and less transparency about which model produced an answer. It also raises a governance question: if every firm runs its own models, auditability and consistent quality become harder to standardise.
report.tools: To follow this trend, watch Nvidia DGX/HGX systems and NIM microservices, plus open serving stacks like vLLM, Hugging Face Text Generation Inference and Ollama for private deployment. Open-weight models such as Llama 3.1/3.3, Mistral and Qwen are the usual base for self-hosting, paired with RAG frameworks like LangChain or LlamaIndex and vector stores such as pgvector and Qdrant. On the legal side, compare Harvey, Legora, Thomson Reuters CoCounsel and Spellbook to see how vendors respond to clients who now own their own GPUs.
